questions.stem: Which finger of the left hand gives the direction of the FORCE?

options.explanation: First finger field, second finger current, thumb force.
The first finger carries the field direction.
The second finger carries the current direction.
The palm plays no role in the rule.

questions.stem: The FIRST finger in Fleming's left-hand rule points along:

options.explanation: Electron flow runs opposite to the conventional current.

options.text: the magnetic field, north to south
options.explanation: Field is assigned to the first finger.
Current belongs to the second finger.
Force belongs to the thumb.

questions.stem: A wire carries current at right angles to a field. The rule predicts the force direction. What is assumed about the current used in the rule?

options.explanation: Direction, not magnitude, is what the rule needs.
There is no separate 'resistance current'.

options.text: the conventional current, from positive to negative
options.explanation: The rule uses conventional current, not electron flow.
Electrons run against the second finger.

questions.stem: The current in the wire is reversed while the field stays fixed. What does the rule now predict?

options.explanation: The prediction flips with the current.

options.text: a larger force in the same direction
options.explanation: Reversal changes direction, not size.
The wire still crosses the field, so a force remains.

options.text: a force in the opposite direction
options.explanation: Reversing one input mirrors the predicted force.

questions.stem: Which arrangement is NOT the perpendicular case that the rule predicts?

options.text: a wire carrying current parallel to the field lines
options.explanation: The rule predicts forces for currents perpendicular to the field.

options.text: a wire carrying current across the field
options.explanation: That is exactly the case the rule covers.

options.text: a wire between two opposite poles
options.explanation: The gap field is a standard case for the rule.

options.text: a straight wire rather than a coil
options.explanation: The rule works wire by wire, straight or coiled.

questions.stem: State what each of the three fingers represents in the left-hand rule.
questions.modelAnswer: First finger along the magnetic field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force.

questions.stem: State which hand is used in the rule for motor-effect force prediction.
questions.modelAnswer: The left hand is used for predicting the force in the motor effect.

questions.stem: Explain why reversing the field direction flips the predicted force.
questions.modelAnswer: The three directions form a right-angled set: with the current unchanged, pointing the first finger the opposite way leaves the thumb pointing the opposite way too. The geometry of the hand mirrors the physics — the force depends on both inputs, so flipping either flips the result.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire runs north, carrying current northwards, in a field directed from east to west. Predict the initial force direction using the rule.
questions.modelAnswer: First finger points west (field), second finger points north (current), and the left-hand thumb then points vertically upwards — the wire is pushed up out of its position.
